## Paper and figure

Delavaux, C. S., Crowther, T. W., Bever, J. D., Weigelt, P., & Gora, E. M. (2024). Mutualisms weaken the latitudinal diversity gradient among oceanic islands. *Nature*, **627**, 335–339. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07110-y>.

I reconstruct **Figure 4** ([original figure and caption](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10937366/figure/Fig4/)). It has three columns for pollination, mycorrhizal association, and nitrogen fixation. The upper panels (a, c, e) show mainland species richness, and the lower panels (b, d, f) show contributions to the island species deficit. Points show observations, lines show predictions, and shaded bands show standard errors. I chose this figure because its panels connect variation in species richness to the composition of species missing from islands.

It meets four criteria: **facets**, **multiple geometric layers**, **group mapped to color**, and **computed smooths with uncertainty bands**. Both axes remain on linear scales, as in the original.

## Part 1: Infer the data

### Variables and observations

The figure requires a location's absolute latitude, a mutualism type, a group within that type, and a response. Mainland species richness is a species count. Contribution to the island deficit is a group's missing species divided by the total missing species, rather than the fraction missing within that group.

| Variable | Type | Simulated values or plausible range |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | Identifier | Integers identifying 180 synthetic comparison locations |
| `latitude` | Continuous | Absolute latitude, 0–70 degrees |
| `type` | Categorical | Pollination, Mycorrhiza, N-fixation |
| `group` | Categorical | Biotic/Abiotic; AM/EM/NM; N-fixing/Non-N-fixing |
| `metric` | Categorical | Mainland richness or deficit contribution |
| `value` | Discrete count or continuous proportion | Nonnegative species counts, usually below 10,000; or proportions from 0 to 1 |

AM and EM mean arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal association; NM means non-mycorrhizal. I generate 180 locations for every group and both metrics: seven groups, six panels, and 2,520 plotted observations. These are simulation choices, not the paper's sample sizes.

### Generating data from the figure

Use the same 180 latitudes drawn uniformly from 0 to 70 degrees for each group. Specify approximate mean responses at every ten degrees using the tables below, then interpolate linearly between those values. These anchor values are my visual approximations, not digitized observations or estimates supplied by the authors.

| Group | 0° | 10° | 20° | 30° | 40° | 50° | 60° | 70° |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Biotic | 1450 | 1650 | 1450 | 900 | 700 | 800 | 450 | 150 |
| Abiotic | 15 | 20 | 30 | 50 | 110 | 170 | 150 | 50 |
| AM | 2600 | 3000 | 2800 | 2000 | 1500 | 1300 | 700 | 350 |
| EM | 10 | 15 | 25 | 40 | 80 | 140 | 100 | 40 |
| NM | 20 | 25 | 30 | 50 | 110 | 160 | 130 | 60 |
| N-fixing | 180 | 240 | 260 | 180 | 130 | 90 | 40 | 10 |
| Non-N-fixing | 140 | 180 | 160 | 150 | 260 | 350 | 260 | 120 |

For richness, add independent normal noise with standard deviation equal to 70% of the interpolated mean, round to whole species, and replace negative counts with zero. The changing noise level makes the scatter wider where richness is higher.

| Group | 0° | 10° | 20° | 30° | 40° | 50° | 60° | 70° |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Biotic | .98 | .98 | .96 | .93 | .85 | .75 | .63 | .50 |
| Abiotic | .02 | .02 | .04 | .07 | .15 | .25 | .37 | .50 |
| AM | .85 | .88 | .89 | .87 | .83 | .77 | .69 | .60 |
| EM | .015 | .020 | .020 | .025 | .030 | .040 | .060 | .080 |
| NM | .135 | .100 | .090 | .105 | .140 | .190 | .250 | .320 |
| N-fixing | .50 | .58 | .60 | .53 | .33 | .16 | .07 | .04 |
| Non-N-fixing | .50 | .42 | .40 | .47 | .67 | .84 | .93 | .96 |

For contributions, add independent uniform noise between −0.04 and 0.04 to the interpolated values. Replace weights below 0.001 with 0.001, then divide by their sum within each location and mutualism type. Thus each set of group contributions sums to one.

These settings reproduce the main relationships: biotic and AM richness peak at low latitudes; the non-N-fixing richness curve has a later peak; biotic and AM deficit contributions decline toward high latitudes; and the two N-fixation contribution curves cross near the middle of the latitude range.

### Simplifications

I use synthetic data and reuse the same latitude design across metrics instead of modelling separate mainland and island samples. The three mutualism types are simulated independently, without forcing their richness totals to agree. I generate contributions directly rather than reconstructing island inventories, and constrain them to nonnegative proportions. I omit spatial dependence and environmental covariates. Local regression (`loess`) replaces the paper's models, while retaining a fitted curve and a band of one standard error. The band describes uncertainty in the fitted mean, not the spread of individual observations. I retain the original circular points, solid curves, panel arrangement, and group-to-color mappings, but use a colorblind-friendly palette.

## Part 2: Rebuild the figure

### Seeded simulation

Only `ggplot2` and `colorspace` are needed in addition to Quarto's R dependencies. The anchor tables make the simulation easy to adjust without fitting the original ecological models.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
seed <- 5014L
set.seed(seed)
library(ggplot2)
n <- 180L
knots <- seq(0, 70, 10)
groups <- c("Biotic", "Abiotic", "AM", "EM", "NM", "N-fixing", "Non-N-fixing")
types <- c("Pollination", "Pollination", rep("Mycorrhiza", 3), rep("N-fixation", 2))
richness <- rbind(
  c(1450,1650,1450,900,700,800,450,150), c(15,20,30,50,110,170,150,50),
  c(2600,3000,2800,2000,1500,1300,700,350), c(10,15,25,40,80,140,100,40),
  c(20,25,30,50,110,160,130,60), c(180,240,260,180,130,90,40,10),
  c(140,180,160,150,260,350,260,120))
shares <- rbind(
  c(.98,.98,.96,.93,.85,.75,.63,.50), c(.02,.02,.04,.07,.15,.25,.37,.50),
  c(.85,.88,.89,.87,.83,.77,.69,.60), c(.015,.020,.020,.025,.030,.040,.060,.080),
  c(.135,.100,.090,.105,.140,.190,.250,.320), c(.50,.58,.60,.53,.33,.16,.07,.04),
  c(.50,.42,.40,.47,.67,.84,.93,.96))
latitude <- runif(n, 0, 70)
dat <- data.frame()
for (j in seq_along(groups)) {
  mu <- approx(knots, richness[j, ], xout = latitude)$y
  weight <- approx(knots, shares[j, ], xout = latitude)$y
  z <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n), latitude, type = types[j], group = groups[j])
  dat <- rbind(dat,
    transform(z, metric = "richness", value = pmax(0, round(rnorm(n, mu, .7 * mu)))),
    transform(z, metric = "contribution", value = pmax(.001, weight + runif(n, -.04, .04))))
}
i <- dat$metric == "contribution"
dat$value[i] <- dat$value[i] / ave(dat$value[i], dat$id[i], dat$type[i], FUN = sum)
panel_names <- c("a  Pollination\nMainland richness (species)",
                 "c  Mycorrhiza\nMainland richness (species)",
                 "e  N-fixation\nMainland richness (species)",
                 "b  Pollination\nDeficit contribution (proportion)",
                 "d  Mycorrhiza\nDeficit contribution (proportion)",
                 "f  N-fixation\nDeficit contribution (proportion)")
panel_id <- match(dat$type, unique(types)) + ifelse(dat$metric == "richness", 0, 3)
dat$panel <- factor(panel_names[panel_id], levels = panel_names)
dat$group <- factor(dat$group, levels = groups)
```

### Smooth curves and standard errors

`loess()` follows the local trend without requiring a single quadratic shape for the whole curve. The loop repeats the same fit for each panel and group. `predict()` returns fitted means and their standard errors; adding and subtracting that standard error gives the ribbon boundaries. Predictions stay within the simulated latitude range, avoiding extrapolation.

```{r}
#| label: smooth-curves
curves <- data.frame()
for (g in groups) {
  for (m in c("richness", "contribution")) {
    z <- subset(dat, group == g & metric == m)
    model <- loess(value ~ latitude, data = z, span = 0.45)
    grid <- data.frame(latitude = seq(min(z$latitude), max(z$latitude), length.out = 100))
    estimate <- predict(model, newdata = grid, se = TRUE)
    curves <- rbind(curves, data.frame(grid, panel = z$panel[1], group = g,
      value = estimate$fit, lower = estimate$fit - estimate$se.fit,
      upper = estimate$fit + estimate$se.fit))
  }
}
curves$panel <- factor(curves$panel, levels = panel_names)
curves$group <- factor(curves$group, levels = groups)
```

### Reconstructed figure

The plotting block uses the same ribbon, scatter, and line layers in every panel. Each panel has its own vertical scale, as in the original. Group labels and units appear in the legend and panel headings.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reconstruction
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
palette <- c(Biotic = "#CC79A7", Abiotic = "#737373", AM = "#0072B2",
             EM = "#E69F00", NM = "#737373", "N-fixing" = "#009E73",
             "Non-N-fixing" = "#737373")
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(latitude, value, color = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = curves, aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, fill = group),
              alpha = 0.20, color = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = curves, linewidth = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = palette) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 20), expand = expansion(mult = 0.03)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Absolute latitude (degrees)", y = NULL, color = "Plant group") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
        panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.2, "lines")) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
p
```

::: {.figure-caption}
**Figure.** Simulated reconstruction of the selected published figure using `r n` synthetic locations, `r length(groups)` groups nested within `r length(unique(types))` mutualism types, and `r nrow(dat)` observations across `r nlevels(dat$panel)` panels. Circular points show simulated observations; solid curves are local regression fits; ribbons extend `r 1L` standard error above and below the fitted mean. The smoothing span is `r 0.45`. Seed: `r seed`. Richness is measured in species, contribution is a dimensionless proportion, and absolute latitude is measured in degrees; these are not the paper's observations.
:::

### Colorblindness check

Only groups within a mutualism type need to be distinguished: pink versus gray for pollination, blue/orange/gray for mycorrhiza, and green versus gray for N-fixation. The swatches below show the actual colors under full-severity simulations of protanopia, deuteranopia, and tritanopia. Reusing gray across different columns does not encode an extra group within any one panel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-palette-check
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.2
colors <- c("#CC79A7", "#737373", "#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73")
vision <- list(Original = identity, Protanopia = colorspace::protan,
               Deuteranopia = colorspace::deutan, Tritanopia = colorspace::tritan)
op <- par(mar = c(1, 9, 1, 1))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, length(colors)), ylim = c(0, 4))
for (i in seq_along(vision)) {
  rect(0:4, 4 - i, 1:5, 4.8 - i, col = vision[[i]](colors), border = NA)
  text(0, 4.4 - i, names(vision)[i], pos = 2, xpd = NA)
}
par(op)
```

## One improvement to the original

The original could use more distinct, colorblind-friendly colors for the mycorrhizal groups to make their overlapping curves easier to distinguish.
